projects.title: Unforced Error
projects.tagline: 19,203 app-store reviews of racquet-sport apps, screened and coded like a systematic review.
projects.blurb: Every app in the racquet-sport corner of the App Store and Google Play, found by keyword, screened against a published rule, and its reviews coded by a codebook you can edit on the page — change a regular expression and all 19,203 reviews recode. The finding: nothing that costs an app stars is a feature. Login, price, crashes and ads sit up to two stars below the corpus mean, while the topics that turn up in the happiest reviews are the ones a product manager files as complaints — doubles support, a watch app, a CSV export. People ask you for features at four and five stars. They leave one star over a login that will not take. Half the build failed and is documented: Apple 403'd its review feed and four other routes to the same text were tried and closed.

projects.title: Thirty-Seven Waves
projects.tagline: Every US tide gauge taken apart into the 37 waves it is made of, and put back together in the browser.
projects.blurb: NOAA publishes, for each of its tide gauges, the amplitude and phase of thirty-seven waves — the moon twice a day, the sun, the moon's elliptical orbit, the tilt of the earth, and ten shallow-water distortions that are not astronomy at all. Add them up and you have the tide, for any date, with no measurement of the ocean. This page ships those coefficients for 1,303 gauges and does the adding itself: a map with no coastline in it, where the country appears because the gauges are on the water; an instrument that switches the waves on one at a time so you can watch the tide assemble; and eight days when the sum was wrong, where subtracting the moon from the record leaves the storm — Isabel putting 7.9 ft of unexpected water into the Potomac at Washington, Sandy 9.3 ft at the Battery, Ian pulling 5.8 ft out of Tampa Bay. The model agrees with NOAA's own tide tables to about a minute and a hundredth of a foot, but it did not start there: it was right in 2026 and 90 minutes wrong in 2003, and finding out why meant measuring NOAA's node factors across a full 18.6-year cycle and discovering a single mis-remembered astronomical constant.

projects.title: Headwaters
projects.tagline: Open data sources, described well enough to use from a shell — and probed, so the catalogue knows what still answers.
projects.blurb: Forty open data sources, each one a JSON record with its licence, auth, rate limit, the traps that cost an hour, copy-pasteable recipes, and — the part nobody else keeps — small real requests with stated expectations that a script re-runs to prove the endpoint still works. Building it turned up six live failures nothing else documents: data.gov's CKAN API 404s on every documented path while its API gateway authenticates your key and redirects you to the dead origin; NOAA's GHCN station list and SWPC's solar-wind feed both moved; Jeff Sackmann's tennis_atp and tennis_wta, the basis of most public tennis analytics, are gone; the Census API without a key returns an HTML page with HTTP 200 so the failure reaches you as a JSON parse error; and the GitHub contents API silently caps a directory at 1,000 entries, which hid 199 datasets from this repository's own first harvest. A companion harvester pulls 3,600 candidates from Data Is Plural, TidyTuesday and the AWS open-data registry into a queue to work through.

projects.title: Still Cited
projects.tagline: What the literature did after each paper was withdrawn.
projects.blurb: Every retraction Retraction Watch has catalogued — 72,389 notices — joined by DOI to OpenAlex citation histories. A field of 72,000 marks plots each paper's publication date against how long it survived; facets slice by reason, journal, publisher, country and field; any mark opens the paper, its original reason codes and its DOI. Of the 39,030 papers whose full citation history is observable, 69% were cited again after the year they were retracted, and 34% of every citation they ever collected arrived after the notice.

projects.title: At Large
projects.tagline: A century of American newspapers reporting animals on the loose.
projects.blurb: There is no dataset of animals escaping from zoos, so this builds one out of full-text search over Chronicling America — the Library of Congress archive of digitised American newspapers. 3,413 pages from 20 period phrasings, 1758–1963, filterable by phrase, animal, decade and state, each linking to the scanned page with the term highlighted. The intended plan was to mine the OCR for what escaped and what happened next; that failed, for a reason the page explains and turns into its subject.

projects.title: Overhead
projects.tagline: 721 real satellites, propagated live in your browser from their orbital elements.
projects.blurb: A draggable day/night globe with coastlines and ground tracks, a time scrubber running up to 3000×, and an altitude-by-inclination census that exposes the hidden structure of the sky. Rather than freezing satellite positions, it ships the orbital elements and solves Kepler's equation in the page, so it stays live indefinitely with no network. Every number drills down to the six elements behind it, and objects on wild ellipses are drawn as perigee-to-apogee lines instead of points.

projects.title: Daybook
projects.tagline: Eighty-five years of daily weather, drawn as a strip chart and played as sound.
projects.blurb: Three NOAA stations within 21 km of one another, one hairline per day from that morning's low to that afternoon's high, inked by departure from normal — and then played out loud. Pitch is temperature, the high voice is the afternoon and the low voice is the overnight, rain is filtered noise and snow a chime. Underneath runs a drone tracking the five-year trailing anomaly: mute everything else and the trend becomes a bass note that climbs across the century. At every station the overnight low rose two to three times faster than the afternoon high.

projects.title: Mermaid Medic
projects.tagline: A linter and live renderer for Mermaid architecture diagrams.
projects.blurb: Paste a .mmd file and get it checked against a strict convention set — quoted labels, safe node IDs, balanced subgraph/end, no stray fences — then rendered live. One-click auto-fix repairs violations, including renaming an unsafe ID everywhere it appears across both node definitions and edges, which is the failure that silently breaks a diagram.

projects.title: GOAT Synthesis
projects.tagline: The men's tennis GOAT debate, run as a systematic review.
projects.blurb: Five Masters-era greats scored across eight criteria of real ATP data, with weight-the-evidence sliders that re-rank the field live, preset lenses for each common argument, and a Monte-Carlo sensitivity analysis over 10,000 random weightings. The honest result is baked in rather than rigged: by the recorded numbers one player wins in 99.9% of weightings, and the interesting part is what the numbers don't capture.

sources.name: ATP records, web-verified at build time
